title: Signal · Monday 23 November
overview: After a quiet weekend, a mathematician's claim to have proved the Riemann hypothesis with Claude, the UBS capital bill reaching a National Council committee and OpenAI's proposal for measuring AI progress lead this morning.

top.headline: An Anthropic mathematician says he proved the Riemann hypothesis with Claude
top.summary: Levent Alpöge, a mathematician at Anthropic, said on 20 November that working with Claude he had found a proof of the Riemann hypothesis and its generalised form, formalised in the Lean proof language. Several mathematicians, including MIT's Andrew Sutherland, confirmed that the Lean code compiles, according to TechCrunch. The same day Stanford's Ravi Vakil posted a separate, proposed proof of the generalised hypothesis by postdoc Alessandro Masullo, which he said is all human, with no AI.
top.background: The hypothesis, posed in 1859, concerns how prime numbers are distributed and is one of the Millennium Prize problems. Lean lets a computer check every step of a proof.
top.why: If it holds, it is the clearest evidence yet that frontier models can contribute original research, and it shows machine checking as the way such output earns trust.
top.watch_next: Whether mathematicians can follow the argument, which Alpöge says is very long and which he intends to write up properly.

top.headline: UBS capital bill reaches a National Council committee as economists dispute UBS's case
top.summary: The National Council's economic affairs committee takes up the capital bill for UBS on 23 and 24 November. Over the weekend three economists quoted by the SonntagsZeitung rejected the arguments UBS published on 19 November, according to the AWP press review. Geneva's Harald Hau said the claim of a competitive disadvantage has no basis in economics, and ETH's Michael Graf said UBS is simply too big for Switzerland.
top.why: The committee's position sets how much extra capital UBS must hold before the bill reaches the full chamber, and with it the bank's room for buybacks.
top.background: UBS and the Swiss Bankers Association rejected key parts of the Federal Council's banking stability package on 19 November. Basel's Heinz Zimmermann said capital costs would rise, but far less than UBS argued.
top.watch_next: The committee's decision and its vote count once the session ends on 24 November.

top.headline: OpenAI's chief scientist proposes perplexity as the yardstick for limits on AI progress
top.summary: In a post on 22 November, Jakub Pachocki, OpenAI's chief scientist, argued that perplexity, a measure of how well a model predicts the next token, should become the shared metric for comparing developers and informing common safety standards. He published OpenAI's internal measurements, a log-perplexity of about 0.91 for GPT-4 and below 0.8 now, the level at which he says new capabilities emerged in cybersecurity and mathematics.
top.background: According to TechCrunch, Anthropic's chief executive Dario Amodei has called for common safety standards and limits on the rate of unchecked AI progress, and Sam Altman called Pachocki's post the most important thing OpenAI has published in a while.
top.why: Any agreed pace needs an agreed measure. If the labs adopt one, the timing of new model generations becomes easier to plan for at firms that build on them.
top.watch_next: Whether Anthropic and Google publish comparable figures.

items.headline: Standard Bank automates risk assessments of its generative AI use cases with AWS
items.summary: Standard Bank Group scores each generative AI use case against international AI standards and its own policies with an automated assessment built with AWS Professional Services, AWS said on 20 November. A model on Amazon Bedrock checks the evidence, an approach called LLM-as-a-judge, and the risk committee still decides, now on evidence gathered the same way for every use case.
items.why: Approval, more than building, is now the bottleneck for bank AI, and a named African bank has shown a way to industrialise the evidence its committees need.

items.headline: Payhawk raises USD 280 million at a USD 2 billion valuation for finance agents
items.summary: The spend management firm's Series C was led by Growth Equity at Goldman Sachs Alternatives, Fintech News Switzerland reported on 20 November. Payhawk plans what it calls a Finance Operating System, in which AI agents do finance work under enterprise controls, and says 77 percent of its customers use its agents daily.
items.why: Corporate finance teams are handing payments work to agents, so banks serving them will meet more agent-initiated transactions and requests for agent-ready payment controls.

items.headline: Most asset managers say onboarding one wealth distributor takes three months or more
items.summary: Among asset managers distributing private market funds through wealth managers and private banks, 58 percent said onboarding a single distributor takes three months or more, according to a Titanbay survey reported by WealthBriefing on 20 November. Titanbay also found that 55 percent of asset managers still run most core fund processes, including subscriptions, capital calls and know-your-customer checks, manually or by email and spreadsheet.
items.why: Private banks pushing semi-liquid private market funds to clients depend on processes that are still largely manual, which leaves room for automation.

items.headline: Fedpol investigator calls for a Swiss register of bank accounts
items.summary: Urs Geier, head of the state security and criminal organisations division at the Federal Office of Police, told the NZZ am Sonntag that Switzerland needs a bank account register on the European model, according to the AWP press review. It would show in one click at which banks suspect people or companies hold accounts. He said Switzerland lags behind European rules.
items.why: A register would change how banks answer requests from police and prosecutors, and it would reopen the debate on banking secrecy.

items.headline: Swiss structured products turnover slips to CHF 62 billion in the third quarter
items.summary: The largest members of the Swiss Structured Products Association turned over CHF 62 billion from July to September, up from CHF 53 billion a year earlier but down from CHF 67 billion in the second quarter and CHF 79 billion in the first, finews reported on 20 November. Yield enhancement products made up 53 percent, led by reverse convertibles at CHF 17 billion.
items.why: Issuers and private banks have lost some momentum after a strong first half, with income products still carrying the market.

items.headline: Close Brothers grows its loan book and holds its motor finance provision
items.summary: The London-listed lender said its underlying loan book grew 1.5 percent in the three months to 31 October, the first quarter of its 2027 financial year, WealthBriefing reported on 20 November. Its provision for motor finance commissions stayed at about GBP 320 million as legal challenges to the regulator's redress scheme continue, and its CET1 ratio held at 14.1 percent.
items.why: A steady provision suggests no new charge while the FCA's motor finance redress scheme is contested, a cost UK lenders are still waiting to size.

items.headline: OpenAI cuts the success of reasoning-extraction attacks from 54 to 0.2 percent
items.summary: OpenAI set out on 20 November how it detects and disrupts adversarial distillation, the unauthorised use of a model's outputs to train a copy without its safeguards. It said that in an internal test, the success rate of attacks recovering protected reasoning fell from 54.0 percent against GPT-6 Astra with its original safeguards to 0.2 percent against GPT-6.2 Astra with its updated safeguards.
items.why: Copies trained on extracted outputs would carry cyber skills without the original's refusals, a risk for banks already facing AI-assisted intrusion tools.

items.headline: AWS releases Textract Insights, document extraction with confidence scores and page references
items.summary: Amazon Textract Insights became generally available on 20 November. Users describe the fields they want in plain language and submit a document or a mixed packet of up to 3,000 pages, and each value comes back with a confidence score and page-level grounding, with no model training. AWS cites mortgage files, claims and onboarding packages as typical uses.
items.why: Credit and onboarding teams can see which values to accept automatically and which to send for review, the evidence auditors ask for when AI reads documents.

items.headline: Suspected Chinese spies exploited a critical VMware vCenter flaw from September
items.summary: A suspected China-linked espionage group, Armory Castle, used a then unknown flaw in VMware vCenter from early September to bypass sign-in and gain administrator rights, Netzwoche reported on 20 November, citing BleepingComputer and Google Mandiant. Broadcom rates the flaw 9.8 out of 10 and has released updates. The group first entered networks through a zero-day in BeyondTrust Remote Support.
items.why: vCenter manages the virtual servers in many bank data centres, and the attackers got around multi-factor sign-in, so the patch cannot wait for a routine window.

say_it_today: The Riemann claim came with a machine-checkable version, and that is what let outsiders test it straight away. For banks deciding how far to trust AI output, work that can be checked step by step is the standard to ask for.
